Variables & Types.exp: Variables and data types in TypeScript.

What is TypeScript: TypeScript is JavaScript with types — not a new language. Baumgartner in 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons' emphasizes: 'TypeScript is about describing the shape of data, not about strict rules'. It adds a compile-time type system on top of JS that's erased at runtime. The key insight: TypeScript's type system is structural (shapes match if they have the same properties) NOT nominal (like Java/C# where names matter). This means you can pass an object matching an interface without explicitly implementing it — it 'fits' the shape. Think of types as documentation that the compiler enforces.
Type Annotations: Annotations tell TypeScript what type you expect. Baumgartner advises: 'let TypeScript infer where it can, annotate where it needs to'. Inference works for initialization (let x = 5 → number) and return types. Annotate function parameters always (they can't be inferred from the caller) and complex return types for documentation. A key lesson from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': annotating too much is as problematic as annotating too little — let inference work, but be explicit at module boundaries (exports, API contracts).
Basic Types: TypeScript's basic types mirror JavaScript: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, void, never, any, bigint, symbol. void means the function returns nothing useful (actually returns undefined). never means the function never returns (always throws or infinite loop). Common mistake: assuming null/undefined are assignable to every type — with strictNullChecks, they must be explicitly unioned. Best practice: enable strictNullChecks; use void for callback return types that may be ignored; use never for exhaustive checks in switch statements.
unknown vs any: any disables type checking entirely — it's an escape hatch that should be avoided. unknown is the type-safe counterpart: you must narrow it via typeof, instanceof, or type guards before use. Common mistake: using any instead of unknown when the type truly isn't known.
Enums: Enums define named constants. Numeric enums auto-increment from 0 and have reverse mappings (value → name). String enums require explicit values and have no reverse mapping. const enum is inlined at compile time (zero runtime cost) but can't be used with isolatedModules or bundlers. Common mistake: assuming enums are just strings — numeric enums have bidirectional mappings which adds runtime code. Best practice: prefer string enums for readability and serialization; use const enum for performance-critical numeric constants; consider union of string literals as a simpler alternative.
Type Inference: TypeScript infers types from values when no annotation is given. Inference works for variable initialization, return values, and generic calls. A common mistake is assuming inference is always correct — complex scenarios may need explicit annotations for clarity.
Literal Types: Literal types restrict a variable to an exact string, number, or boolean value. Combine with union types for constrained options. A common mistake is thinking any string matching the literal format is assignable — the value must be exactly the literal.

type Direction = 'up' | 'down' | 'left' | 'right'; // creates reusable type alias
let dir: Direction = 'up'; // declares variable with explicit type
dir = 'diagonal'; // Error

type Port = 80 | 443 | 8080; // creates reusable type alias
const port: Port = 443; // declares variable with explicit type
Strict Mode: Enable strict: true in tsconfig to activate all strict checks: noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, and alwaysStrict. A common mistake is starting a project without strict mode and adding it later — much harder to migrate.

Typed Error Classes: Create custom Error subclasses with typed properties. Set the name property for proper instanceof checks. A common mistake is forgetting to set error.name — without it, instanceof may work inconsistently across inheritance chains.
Try/Catch with unknown: In strict mode, catch variables are unknown, not any. Narrow them with instanceof, typeof, or custom guards. A common mistake is accessing err.message without checking — TypeScript will error with 'Object is of type unknown'.
Result Types: Result types model success/failure without exceptions using a discriminated union. This forces callers to handle both paths explicitly. A common mistake is using exceptions for expected failure modes instead of modeling them in the type system.
Definite Assignment Assertions: Use the ! assertion (!:) to tell TypeScript that a variable is definitely assigned, even when the compiler can't prove it. Common in class properties initialized in constructor helpers or lifecycle methods. A common mistake is overusing it to silence warnings instead of restructuring code.
Null Checks: With strictNullChecks, null and undefined are distinct types. Use optional chaining (?.), nullish coalescing (??), and type guards to handle nullable values safely. A common mistake is using || instead of ?? for defaults — || treats empty string and 0 as falsy.
Result Pattern & Discriminated Unions: Functional error handling with Result types: `type Result<T, E = Error> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }`. Pattern match on `.ok`. Never type for exhaustive checks. Discriminated unions for domain errors. Either type from fp-ts or custom. Combine with type guards. Avoids try/catch sprawl — composable error handling. Use branded types for compile-time safety.

Input/Output.exp: Input and output operations in TypeScript.

Union Types: Unions express 'either this type OR that type'. Baumgartner says: 'union types are TypeScript's most powerful feature — they model reality where data comes in multiple shapes'. The best part: TypeScript forces you to NARROW the type before using type-specific operations. This eliminates entire categories of runtime errors. Narrowing happens through typeof, instanceof, in, discriminated property checks, or custom type guards. A key insight from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': always use discriminated unions (a common literal property like kind) for clear, exhaustive type narrowing — they're the backbone of TypeScript error handling patterns.
Intersection Types: Intersection types combine multiple types into one, requiring all properties from each type. Use & to merge object types. A common mistake is intersecting primitives (like string & number), which results in never.

type HasName = { name: string }; // creates reusable type alias
type HasAge = { age: number }; // creates reusable type alias
type Person = HasName & HasAge; // creates reusable type alias
const p: Person = { name: 'Alice', age: 30 }; // declares variable with explicit type
// type Impossible = string & number; // never
Type Aliases: Type aliases name a type for reuse. Baumgartner: 'use type for unions, intersections, and tuples; use interface for object shapes you might extend'. type can represent anything (primitives, unions, tuples, objects); interface is restricted to objects. The key difference: interfaces can be declaration-merged (reopened and extended), types cannot. A lesson from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': prefer interface for public API contracts (they're more discoverable in editor tooltips and error messages), use type for complex type expressions.
Interfaces: Interfaces define the shape of objects. Baumgartner in 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons' highlights: 'interfaces are open — they can be extended via declaration merging'. This makes them ideal for library types that users might want to augment. Interfaces also extend cleanly (extends), can be implemented in classes, and produce better error messages. A critical insight: interfaces evaluate lazily (they don't resolve all members immediately), while type aliases evaluate eagerly. This matters for recursive types — interfaces handle them naturally, types need explicit indirection.
Structural Typing: TypeScript uses structural (duck) typing: type compatibility is determined by shape, not name. Two types with identical members are interchangeable. A common mistake is expecting nominal typing behavior where type names should differ.

interface Point { x: number; y: number; } // defines object shape contract
interface Coord { x: number; y: number; } // defines object shape contract
const p: Point = { x: 1, y: 2 }; // declares variable with explicit type
const c: Coord = p; // OK: same structure

class Car { drive() {} } // defines a class blueprint
class Boat { drive() {} } // defines a class blueprint
const v: Car = new Boat(); // OK: same shape
Type Assertions: Type assertions (as) tell TypeScript you know more about a type than it does. They do not perform runtime checks. A common mistake is using assertions to silence errors instead of fixing the real type issue. Prefer 'as' over angle-bracket syntax in JSX.
Branded Types: Branded types add a phantom property to simulate nominal typing. This prevents mixing structurally compatible types like UserId and OrderId. A common mistake is forgetting that brands are compile-time only — they have no runtime effect.

type UserId = string & { readonly __brand: 'UserId' }; // creates reusable type alias
type OrderId = string & { readonly __brand: 'OrderId' }; // creates reusable type alias
function getUser(id: UserId) { /* ... */ } // defines reusable function block
const uid = 'abc123' as UserId; // declares variable with type assertion
getUser(uid); // calls function with arguments
// getUser('abc123'); // Error: not branded
satisfies Operator: The satisfies operator validates that a value matches a type without widening the inferred type. This preserves the narrowest type for autocomplete and type-checking. A common mistake is using a type annotation instead, which widens the type.

typeof Type Guards: typeof narrows primitive types in conditional blocks. TypeScript understands typeof returning 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'symbol', 'bigint', 'undefined', 'object', and 'function'. A common mistake is checking typeof null which returns 'object' — use value === null instead.
instanceof Type Guards: instanceof narrows types based on constructor/prototype chain. Works with classes and built-in constructors like Date, Error, RegExp. A common mistake is using instanceof with interfaces — they are compile-time only and erased at runtime.
Equality Narrowing: Equality checks (===, !==) narrow types by excluding mismatched values. Switch statements and strict equality against literal types narrow to the matching branch. A common mistake is using == instead of === which allows type coercion.
Truthiness Narrowing: Truthiness checks (if, &&, ||, !) narrow types by excluding falsy values: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN. A common mistake is forgetting that empty string '' and 0 are falsy — use ?? for null/undefined only.
Type Predicates: Type predicates (parameterName is Type) are custom type guard return types. They tell TypeScript what a value is when the function returns true. A common mistake is writing a predicate that doesn't actually check — TypeScript trusts your predicate blindly.
Discriminated Unions: Discriminated unions use a common literal property (the discriminant) to narrow each variant. TypeScript understands switch/case and if/else checks on the discriminant. A common mistake is not using a literal type as the discriminant.

Function Types: Function types describe callable signatures: parameter types and return type. Use type aliases or inline syntax. A common mistake is forgetting that callbacks can have optional parameters and void return types are assignable from any return value.

type BinaryFn = (a: number, b: number) => number; // creates reusable type alias
const add: BinaryFn = (x, y) => x + y; // declares variable with explicit type

type LogFn = (msg: string) => void; // creates reusable type alias
const log: LogFn = (msg) => console.log(msg); // declares variable with explicit type
Optional & Default Parameters: Mark parameters as optional with ? or provide default values. Optional params must follow required ones. Default parameters are always optional and infer their type from the default value. A common mistake is mixing up order — optional params can't precede required ones.

function greet(name?: string): string { // defines reusable function block
  return `Hello, ${name ?? 'Guest'}`; // returns value to calling code
}
function multiply(a: number, b: number = 1): number { // defines reusable function block
  return a * b; // returns value to calling code
}
greet();      // 'Hello, Guest'
multiply(5);  // 5
Generic Functions: Generics preserve type information through functions. Baumgartner: 'generics are about describing relationships between types'. The classic example: Array<T> — the type parameter T flows from creation through every method. TypeScript infers T from arguments 90% of the time. Constrain T with extends when you need specific capabilities (like T extends HasLength). A key insight from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': 'generics are contagious' — once you add a type parameter to a function, every function that wraps it likely needs one too. Use multiple type parameters for complex relationships.
Function Overloads: Overloads declare multiple call signatures for a single implementation. The implementation signature must be compatible with all overloads but is not callable directly. A common mistake is having an implementation signature that can't satisfy all overloads.

function combine(a: string, b: string): string; // defines reusable function block
function combine(a: number, b: number): number; // defines reusable function block
function combine(a: any, b: any): any { // defines reusable function block
  return a + b; // returns value to calling code
}
combine('a', 'b'); // string
combine(1, 2);     // number
// combine(1, 'b'); // Error: no matching overload
Rest Parameters: Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an array. Type them as an array type. TypeScript also supports typed tuples for rest parameters in variadic patterns. A common mistake is thinking rest must be the last parameter — it must be the only last parameter.

function sum(...numbers: number[]): number { // defines reusable function block
  return numbers.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // returns value to calling code
}
sum(1, 2, 3, 4); // 10

function logValues(...args: [string, ...number[]]) { // defines reusable function block
  console.log(args[0], args.slice(1)); // outputs message to developer console
}
logValues('scores', 95, 87); // calls function with arguments
this Parameters: TypeScript uses a fake first parameter named 'this' to type the function's context. This catches errors where 'this' is used incorrectly, common in callbacks and event handlers. A common mistake is forgetting to bind 'this' or using arrow functions when a dynamic 'this' is needed.
Async Functions: Async functions always return Promise<T> where T is the resolved type. Annotate the return type as Promise<T> for clarity. A common mistake is forgetting that async functions wrap the returned value in Promise — you must await or .then() to get the value.
void & never Return Types: void means the function completes normally but returns nothing meaningful (actually returns undefined). never means the function never completes — it always throws or loops forever. A common mistake is assigning void to something expecting a value, or thinking never is the same as void.
Nested Loops: Nested loops in TypeScript work like JavaScript but benefit from type safety — the compiler tracks array element types, ensures indices are valid numbers, and catches out-of-bounds when using array types with literal index access. Use for...of with destructuring for cleaner 2D iteration. Prefer flat() and flatMap() for transforming nested structures over manual nested loops when possible.

Classes: TypeScript classes add type annotations to fields, constructors, and methods. Fields must be declared with types or initialized. A common mistake is forgetting to initialize a field or declare it — the strictPropertyInitialization check will catch this.
Inheritance: Use extends to create subclasses. Call super() before accessing this in the constructor. A common mistake is forgetting super() entirely or calling super() after accessing this. Use the override keyword to explicitly mark method overrides.
Access Modifiers: public (default), private, and protected control member visibility. private prevents access outside the class; protected allows access in subclasses. A common mistake is relying on these for runtime security — they are compile-time only and erased at runtime.
Abstract Classes: Abstract classes define shared behavior with abstract methods that subclasses must implement. They cannot be instantiated directly. A common mistake is trying to use new on an abstract class or forgetting to implement all abstract methods in a subclass.
Interfaces with Classes: Classes can implement interfaces to guarantee a shape. A class can implement multiple interfaces. Unlike extends, implements doesn't inherit implementation, only enforces shape. A common mistake is thinking implements provides default implementations — it only enforces type contracts.
Static Members: Static properties and methods belong to the class, not instances. Access them via ClassName.property. A common mistake is trying to access static members through an instance or using this inside a static method to access instance members.
Parameter Properties: Parameter properties combine declaration and assignment in one step. Prefix a constructor parameter with public, private, protected, or readonly to auto-create the field. A common mistake is forgetting that the access modifier is required — without it, it's just a regular parameter, not a property.
Mixins: Mixins compose behavior from multiple classes using constructor type patterns. TypeScript doesn't support multiple inheritance, but mixins provide a composable alternative. A common mistake is not properly typing the constructor return type or forgetting to call super in a mixin.

Generic Types: Generic types parameterize types with type variables, enabling reusable, type-safe containers. Type variables are placeholders for actual types determined at use. A common mistake is not providing enough type parameters or omitting them entirely when inference fails.

type Box<T> = { value: T }; // creates reusable type alias
type Pair<T, U> = { first: T; second: U }; // creates reusable type alias
type Result<T> = { data: T; error?: string }; // creates reusable type alias

const box: Box<number> = { value: 42 }; // declares variable with explicit type
const pair: Pair<string, number> = { first: 'a', second: 1 }; // declares variable with explicit type
Constraints: Use extends to constrain type parameters to types with specific properties. This allows the generic implementation to safely access those properties. A common mistake is not constraining when you need to call methods on the generic value.

interface HasLength { length: number } // defines object shape contract
function logLength<T extends HasLength>(arg: T): number { // defines reusable function block
  console.log(arg.length); // outputs message to developer console
  return arg.length; // returns value to calling code
}
logLength('hello');     // 5
logLength([1, 2, 3]);   // 3
// logLength(123); // Error: number doesn't have length
Utility Types: TypeScript provides built-in utility types: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Record<K,T>, Pick<T,K>, Omit<T,K>, Exclude<T,U>, Extract<T,U>, NonNullable<T>, and more. They reduce boilerplate for common type transformations.
Generic Classes: Generic classes maintain type parameters across all members and methods. The type parameter is fixed at construction time. A common mistake is not specifying the type parameter when creating an instance, causing inference from the constructor args.
Conditional Types: Conditional types select between types based on a condition. Baumgartner calls them 'TypeScript's if/else at the type level'. The structure T extends U ? X : Y. A critical behavior: they DISTRIBUTE over unions — if T is string | number, the conditional applies to each member separately and the results are unioned. The infer keyword captures a type from within a larger type. A lesson from 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons': 'conditional types are the foundation of all advanced TypeScript patterns' — they power ReturnType, Extract, Exclude, and NonNullable. Use them to build type transformations that adapt to the input type.
Mapped Types: Mapped types transform each property of a type using { [K in keyof T]: T[K] }. Add modifiers like ? and readonly to create variations. A common mistake is forgetting that mapped types preserve modifiers by default — use -? and -readonly to remove them.
Template Literal Types: Template literal types construct string types at the type level using embedded type placeholders. Combined with union types, they generate all possible combinations. A common mistake is thinking they work at runtime — they are purely compile-time constructs.

type EventName<T extends string> = `on${Capitalize<T>}`; // creates reusable type alias
type Color = 'red' | 'green' | 'blue'; // creates reusable type alias
type DarkColor = `dark-${Color}`; // creates reusable type alias
// 'dark-red' | 'dark-green' | 'dark-blue'
type ClickEvent = EventName<'click'>; // 'onClick'
type Events = EventName<'click' | 'focus'>; // creates reusable type alias
// 'onClick' | 'onFocus'
infer Keyword: The infer keyword introduces a type variable within a conditional type's extends clause, capturing a type from a larger structure. It powers most advanced utility types like ReturnType. A common mistake is using infer outside a conditional type — it's only valid in the extends clause.

type ReturnType<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never; // creates reusable type alias
type Fn = (x: number) => string; // creates reusable type alias
type R = ReturnType<Fn>; // string

type FirstParam<T> = T extends (first: infer F, ...args: any[]) => any ? F : never; // creates reusable type alias
type P = FirstParam<(name: string, age: number) => void>; // string

type PromiseValue<T> = T extends Promise<infer V> ? V : T; // creates reusable type alias
type PV = PromiseValue<Promise<number>>; // number

Partial<T>: Partial<T> makes all properties of T optional. Useful for update operations where you only supply changed fields. A common mistake is applying Partial to deeply nested objects — it only affects the top level.
Required<T>: Required<T> makes all properties of T required (removes optionality). Useful for transforming optional configs into full required types. A common mistake is forgetting Required does not affect nested optional properties.

interface Config { url?: string; timeout?: number; }
type StrictConfig = Required<Config>;
Readonly<T>: Readonly<T> makes all properties of T readonly. Useful for immutable objects and configs. A common mistake is thinking Readonly prevents deep mutation — use as const or DeepReadonly for nested immutability.
Record<K,T>: Record<K,T> creates an object type with keys K and values T. K is usually a union of string literals. A common mistake is using Record<string, T> when you know the specific keys — prefer a mapped type for better autocomplete.
Pick<T,K>: Pick<T,K> creates a type with only the specified keys K from T. Useful for creating lightweight view types from full data types. A common mistake is picking keys that don't exist on T — TypeScript catches this at compile time.

interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; password: string; }
type PublicUser = Pick<User, 'id' | 'name' | 'email'>;
Omit<T,K>: Omit<T,K> creates a type without the specified keys K from T. The inverse of Pick. Useful for excluding sensitive fields. A common mistake is using Omit when you want to exclude by value type rather than key name.

interface User { id: number; name: string; email: string; password: string; }
type SafeUser = Omit<User, 'password'>;
Exclude<T,U>: Exclude<T,U> removes types from T that are assignable to U. Works with union types. A common mistake is using Exclude for object properties when you should use Omit — Exclude works on union members, not object keys.

type T = string | number | boolean;
type WithoutString = Exclude<T, string>;
Extract<T,U>: Extract<T,U> extracts types from T that are assignable to U. The opposite of Exclude. Useful for filtering union types to a subset. A common mistake is expecting Extract to filter object properties — use Pick instead.

type T = string | number | boolean;
type OnlyString = Extract<T, string>;
NonNullable<T>: NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined from T. Useful for cleaning up after validation. A common mistake is using NonNullable on object types expecting it to remove null properties from fields.

type T = string | number | null | undefined;
type Clean = NonNullable<T>;
ReturnType<T>: ReturnType<T> extracts the return type of a function type T. Uses conditional types with infer internally. A common mistake is passing a function value instead of a type — use typeof to get the type first.
Parameters<T>: Parameters<T> extracts the parameter types of a function type T as a tuple. Useful for forwarding argument types to wrappers. A common mistake is forgetting Parameters returns a tuple, not a union.

function log(name: string, age: number): void {}
type P = Parameters<typeof log>;
Awaited<T>: Awaited<T> unwraps Promise types recursively. Useful for getting the resolved type of async functions. A common mistake is using Awaited on non-Promise types — it passes them through unchanged.

Conditional Types: Advanced conditional types enable type-level branching and filtering. They distribute over unions unless wrapped with brackets. Use them for building utilities like Exclude and Extract. A common mistake is assuming conditionals work at runtime — they are purely compile-time.

type IsArray<T> = T extends any[] ? true : false; // creates reusable type alias
type Check = IsArray<string | number[]>; // boolean (distributed)

type NonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T; // creates reusable type alias
type Clean = NonNullable<string | null | undefined>; // string

type ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never; // creates reusable type alias
type E = ElementType<string[]>; // string
Mapped Types: Advanced mapped types iterate over object keys with keyof. Use the as clause for key remapping and combine with conditional types to filter keys. A common mistake is not accounting for readonly and optional modifiers that are preserved by default.
Indexed Access Types: Indexed access types (T[K]) retrieve the type of a property at key K. Use T[keyof T] for all values or T[number] for array elements. A common mistake is using a key that doesn't exist on the type, which produces a compile-time error.
Type Guards: Type guards narrow types in conditional blocks using x is T predicates. Use typeof, instanceof, or custom functions. A common mistake is writing guards that are too broad or forgetting that in operator also acts as a type guard in TS 5.5+.
Variadic Tuple Types: Variadic tuple types use spread in tuple positions to capture variable-length patterns. They enable strongly typed concatenation, partial application, and parameter forwarding. A common mistake is forgetting that spreads in tuples create new tuple types.
Recursive Types: Recursive types reference themselves to model nested structures like JSON, trees, or linked lists. TypeScript supports recursive type aliases but has depth limits to prevent infinite expansion. A common mistake is creating infinitely recursive types without a base case.
Discriminated Unions: Discriminated unions are TypeScript's most important pattern for modeling state. Baumgartner: 'they make impossible states impossible'. A discriminated union has a common literal property (the discriminant, like kind or status) that tells TypeScript which variant is active. Inside a switch on the discriminant, TypeScript narrows the type to the specific variant. This eliminates entire classes of runtime errors (wrong property access, missing cases). 'TypeScript in 50 Lessons' emphasizes: 'model your data as discriminated unions, not optional fields' — instead of optional error/loading/data fields, use a single union with { status: 'loading' } | { status: 'success', data: T } | { status: 'error', error: string }.
keyof & typeof Operators: keyof T produces a union of the keys of T. typeof x extracts the type of a value at compile time. Combine them for dynamic property access patterns. A common mistake is using typeof at runtime instead of compile-time — typeof at runtime is JavaScript's typeof.

ESM Imports: TypeScript supports ES module import/export syntax. Use import type for type-only imports to avoid runtime overhead. A common mistake is mixing default and named imports incorrectly, or forgetting that type-only imports are erased at compile time.
Namespaces: Namespaces group related code under a global namespace. They are legacy constructs — prefer ES modules for new code. Still useful for ambient declarations and library definitions. A common mistake is mixing namespace and module imports.
Decorators: Decorators modify classes, methods, properties, or parameters. They are experimental in TypeScript (enable experimentalDecorators). Use them for metaprogramming, logging, and dependency injection. A common mistake is forgetting that decorator evaluation order matters.
tsconfig: tsconfig.json configures the TypeScript compiler. Key options: target, module, strict, outDir, rootDir, and lib. A common mistake is not including files in the project or using conflicting module and moduleResolution settings.
Declaration Files: Declaration files (.d.ts) describe JavaScript module shapes without implementation. Use declare module for third-party libs and declare global for augmenting globals. A common mistake is writing implementation code in .d.ts files — they should only contain type declarations.
Triple-Slash Directives: Triple-slash directives are single-line comments referencing other files. Used in declaration files for legacy reference management. Types, path, and lib directives exist. A common mistake is using these in modern projects — prefer ESM imports instead.

Promise Types: Promise<T> represents an asynchronous value. The type parameter T is the resolved type. A common mistake is treating Promise<T> as T — you must await or .then() to unwrap the value. Promise<void> is common for fire-and-forget async operations.
Async/Await: Async functions always return Promise<T>. Await unwraps the promise inside an async function. TypeScript tracks types through await. A common mistake is forgetting to await a promise or wrapping an already-async function in another Promise unnecessarily.
Async Iterators: Async iterators (AsyncIterable<T>) produce values asynchronously. Use for await...of to consume them. Useful for streaming data, paginated APIs, and event streams. A common mistake is using for...of (sync) on an async iterable, which causes a runtime error.
Typed Event Emitters: Typed event emitters use generics to map event names to payload types. This provides type-safe on/emit patterns. A common mistake is not typing the event map, resulting in any-typed event data throughout the codebase.
Promise Combinators: Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.allSettled, and Promise.any have typed return values. TypeScript infers tuples/unions from the input array. A common mistake is assuming Promise.all returns a loose array — it returns a tuple when given a tuple literal.
Error Handling in Async Code: Async errors require try/catch. In strict mode, caught errors are typed as unknown — you must narrow them. A common mistake is assuming the error is always an Error instance or not handling non-Error throws like strings or objects.

Template Literal Types: Template literal types construct string types at compile time using embedded type expressions. Combined with unions, they generate all possible string combinations automatically. A common mistake is assuming these can be used at runtime — they're erased during compilation.
satisfies Operator: satisfies validates a value's type while preserving the narrowest inferred type for autocomplete. Unlike type annotations, it doesn't widen. A common mistake is using a type annotation instead of satisfies, which loses the specific types of individual properties.
Assertion Functions: Assertion functions use the asserts return type to narrow types after a call. They throw if the assertion fails, making subsequent code safe. A common mistake is writing assertion functions without the asserts keyword, which prevents TypeScript from narrowing.

function assertDefined<T>(value: T): asserts value is NonNullable<T> { // defines reusable function block
  if (value === null || value === undefined) { // conditionally executes following block
    throw new Error('Value is null or undefined'); // intentionally raises an error
  }
}
const x: string | null = Math.random() > 0.5 ? 'hello' : null; // declares variable with explicit type
assertDefined(x); // calls function with arguments
console.log(x.toUpperCase()); // x narrowed to string

function assertString(value: unknown): asserts value is string { // defines reusable function block
  if (typeof value !== 'string') throw new Error('Not a string'); // conditionally executes following block
}
Branded Types: Branded types add a unique phantom property to create distinguishable types from structurally identical ones. This prevents mixing values like emails and phone numbers. A common mistake is forgetting to cast at the boundary — brands are not automatically applied.

type Email = string & { readonly __brand: 'Email' }; // creates reusable type alias
type Phone = string & { readonly __brand: 'Phone' }; // creates reusable type alias

function sendEmail(to: Email, body: string): void { // defines reusable function block
  console.log(`Sending to ${to}`); // outputs message to developer console
}

const addr = 'user@example.com' as Email; // declares variable with type assertion
sendEmail(addr, 'hello'); // calls function with arguments

const phone = '555-0100' as Phone; // declares variable with type assertion
// sendEmail(phone, 'hello'); // Error: Phone not assignable to Email

// Factory function as safer boundary:
function createEmail(s: string): Email { // defines reusable function block
  if (!s.includes('@')) throw new Error('Invalid email'); // conditionally executes following block
  return s as Email; // returns value to calling code
}
Nominal Typing: TypeScript uses structural typing by default. To simulate nominal typing (type identity matters), use brands, enum discriminants, or intersection with unique class types. A common mistake is expecting structural typing to catch nominal mismatches automatically.

class Nominal<T> { // defines a class blueprint
  private readonly _brand!: T; // declares access-controlled member
}

type USD = Nominal<{ readonly __type: 'USD' }> & number; // creates reusable type alias
type EUR = Nominal<{ readonly __type: 'EUR' }> & number; // creates reusable type alias

function addMoney(a: USD, b: USD): USD { // defines reusable function block
  return (a + b) as USD; // returns value to calling code
}

const dollars = 100 as USD; // declares variable with type assertion
const euros = 200 as EUR; // declares variable with type assertion
addMoney(dollars, dollars); // OK
// addMoney(dollars, euros); // Error: types don't match
Covariance & Contravariance: Covariance preserves assignment direction (Dog[] is Animal[]). Contravariance reverses it (function parameters). TypeScript is covariant for most types but checks function parameters bivariantly by default — strictFunctionTypes fixes this. A common mistake is expecting array invariance.

Typed DOM APIs: TypeScript includes DOM type definitions. Use specific element types (HTMLInputElement, HTMLCanvasElement) instead of generic Element for type-safe property access. A common mistake is using querySelector without the generic parameter, resulting in an Element type.
Event Typing: DOM events have specific types (MouseEvent, KeyboardEvent, FocusEvent, SubmitEvent) with typed properties. Use addEventListener's generic for proper typing. A common mistake is typing all events as Event, losing access to event-specific properties like clientX or key.
Form Typing: Type form access with HTMLFormElement and HTMLInputElement. FormData provides key-value access. A common mistake is forgetting to check if a form element exists before accessing it, or not casting data.get() results.
Fetch Typing: The fetch API returns Promise<Response>. Parse the body with json(), text(), etc. Type the parsed data, not the fetch call. A common mistake is not checking res.ok or assuming JSON parsing always succeeds.
Typed Fetch & API Clients: Typed fetch wrappers enhance type safety. Generic response typing: `fetch<T>(url): Promise<T>`. Zod for runtime validation: `z.union([z.string(), z.number()])`. Axios with generics: `axios.get<MyType>(url)`. Error handling with typed errors. Interceptors for auth/logging. Type-safe query params, headers, and bodies. Parse JSON to discriminated unions with pattern matching.

Formatting (Prettier): Prettier is the standard TypeScript formatter handling semicolons, quotes, trailing commas, and indentation. Integrate with editor format-on-save and CI checks. A common mistake is Prettier conflicting with ESLint — use eslint-config-prettier to disable formatting rules in ESLint.
Linting (ESLint): ESLint with @typescript-eslint catches TypeScript-specific issues like unused variables, unsafe assertions, and promise handling errors. A common mistake is disabling strict rules like no-explicit-any — prefer incremental fixing.
DefinitelyTyped & @types: DefinitelyTyped is the community repository of TypeScript type definitions. Install with @types/package-name. Most popular libraries now include bundled types. A common mistake is installing @types for a package that already ships its own types.
Build Tools: Modern TypeScript projects often skip tsc for building and use bundlers instead. Vite, tsup, and SWC are popular choices. Use tsc --noEmit for type-checking only and a bundler for output. A common mistake is using tsc for both checking and bundling.
Bun Runtime & Tools: Bun is a fast JavaScript runtime, bundler, test runner, and package manager. Node.js compatible with built-in TypeScript, JSX, ESM, and CommonJS support. Key features: `bun run` (faster than npm), `bun test` (Jest-compatible), `bun build` (bundler), `bunx` (npx replacement). Native APIs: Bun.file(), Bun.write(), Bun.serve() for HTTP servers. SQLite3 built-in: `Bun.sqlite`. Watch mode: `bun --watch`.

Strict Compiler Options: Beyond strict: true, individual strict flags include noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, noImplicitThis, and alwaysStrict. Additional safety: noUncheckedIndexedAccess and exactOptionalPropertyTypes.
Module Resolution: moduleResolution controls how TypeScript resolves imports: classic, node, node16, nodenext, or bundler. bundler is best for modern bundlers like Vite and esbuild. A common mistake is using node with ESNext module output, causing resolution mismatches.
Path Aliases: Path aliases allow cleaner imports by mapping directories to short prefixes. Configure in tsconfig paths and sync with your bundler. A common mistake is setting baseUrl but forgetting to configure the bundler's resolve alias to match.
Project References: Project references split a codebase into independently buildable sub-projects. Each has a tsconfig with composite: true. Improves build performance via incremental compilation and enforces module boundaries. A common mistake is circular references between projects.
Build Modes: Use tsc -b for build mode with project references. It builds all referenced projects in dependency order with incremental compilation. --clean removes build artifacts. A common mistake is running plain tsc instead of tsc -b in a monorepo with references.
ESM vs CJS Deep: ECMAScript Modules (ESM) vs CommonJS (CJS). ESM: `import/export`, static analysis, tree-shaking, top-level await, `import.meta.url`. CJS: `require/module.exports`, dynamic loading, `__dirname`, `__filename`. Package.json `type: "module"` for ESM. `.mjs`/.cjs` extensions force module type. Dual package hazard: `exports` map in package.json for conditional exports. Interop: CJS can `import()` ESM; ESM imports CJS as default export.

LLM API Integration: Call OpenAI/Claude from Node.js with full type safety. Use zod for response validation, handle streaming with AsyncIterable, manage rate limits with p-limit. Common mistake: not validating LLM responses at runtime — JSON parse can fail; always use a schema-based parser.
LangChain.js: LangChain.js brings chains, agents, and retrieval to Node.js/TypeScript with full type safety. Supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, local models, vector stores, and tool integration. Common mistake: not typing chain inputs/outputs — use RunnableWithMessageHistory for typed conversations.
Vercel AI SDK: Vercel AI SDK provides React/Vue/Svelte hooks for streaming LLM responses, tool calling, and structured generation. Framework-agnostic core with React/Vue/Svelte adapters. Handles streaming, abort controllers, error boundaries. Common mistake: using it only with Vercel — it works with any Node.js framework (Express, Fastify).
Embeddings & Vector Search in JS: Generate embeddings from JS (OpenAI, Transformers.js) and search them in vector databases. Chroma.js for local use, pgvector for Postgres, Pinecone for managed. Use worker_threads to avoid blocking the event loop for embedding generation. Common mistake: recomputing embeddings on every query — cache results.
Transformers.js: Run Hugging Face models directly in the browser or Node.js with Transformers.js. No GPU, no Python — pure ONNX runtime in JS. Supports text classification, embeddings, token generation, image classification, speech-to-text. Common mistake: downloading full model weights on every page load — use IndexedDB caching via quantized models.
Browser ML (WebGPU/WebNN): Run ML models in the browser with hardware acceleration. TensorFlow.js for training/inference; ONNX Runtime for cross-framework model deployment; MediaPipe for vision/audio pipelines; WebGPU for GPU compute. Common mistake: assuming all devices support WebGPU — always provide WebGL fallback.
Structured LLM Output with Zod: Combine Zod schemas with LLM calls for type-safe, validated structured output. Zod's discriminated unions power conditional LLM responses; refine/transform validate complex business rules. Integrates with OpenAI structured outputs, Vercel AI SDK tool calls, LangChain withStructuredOutput. Common mistake: making schemas too strict — LLMs need room for variation.
Streaming & Real-time AI: Stream LLM responses over Server-Sent Events or WebSocket for real-time UX. AbortController for cancellation, backpressure handling, reconnection logic. Use ReadableStream for Node.js-to-browser streaming. Common mistake: buffering entire response before sending — defeats purpose of streaming.
AI-Powered Search: Build semantic search with embeddings + vector DB. Hybrid search combines keyword (BM25) with semantic (vector) for best results. Rerank results with cross-encoders. Use Result type pattern for type-safe search responses. Common mistake: ignoring keyword search — pure semantic search misses exact matches.
Building AI Agents in TypeScript: Build AI agents with tool-use, memory, and planning in TypeScript. Use the ReAct pattern (Thought → Action → Observation), maintain conversation history, and execute tools safely. TypeScript's discriminated unions model agent state perfectly. Common mistake: infinite loops — always cap iterations and depth.
